63:

72: For multi-domain, ambiguous, or previously mis-routed requests, load [specialist routing](references/specialist-routing.md) first. It defines the staged selection pipeline, the selection record, cross-domain base-plus-narrow composition, disambiguation of overlapping modules, and orchestration roles. 73: 
74: 1. Exactly one primary specialist owns the deliverable; every other module is supporting with a distinct responsibility or an independent verifier.
75: 2. When a trigger fires and the request is in scope, emit at least one domain specialist name. An empty set after activation is a routing failure. Validate the set against the on-disk reference listing before execution and re-select if it is empty or helper-only.
76: 3. Emit only module names that exist in `skills/rcoder/references/`. Never invent a name from memory.
77: 4. A helper never replaces a domain module and never serves as the primary.
78: 5. For cross-domain work, keep the framing base (for example `security`, `systems-programming`) alongside the narrow technical module; do not substitute one for the other. 79: 6. Where the tables below offer two modules, the first is the default; load the second only when its stated condition holds. Loading both is not the default; record the rejected alternative.
80: 7. Select by deliverable and acceptance criteria rather than English keyword matching. For paraphrased or non-English prompts, restate the required artifact and its check, preserve technical identifiers, and route from that restatement.
81: 
82: Record the selection as: classification · candidates · selected · primary · supporting with reasons · verifier · ordinal confidence · unselected alternatives · required verification · handoff dependencies.
83: 
84: For unfamiliar models or hosts, choose an execution profile before routing; see [model adaptation](references/model-adaptation.md). Host evidence tiers are recorded in `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` and observed runtime facts in `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md`. These documents are host-side metadata, not skills to load for domain tasks.

86: ### Core engineering
87: 
88: | Signal | Reference |
89: |---|---|
90: | Source implementation, compiler/type errors, language idioms | [coding](references/coding.md) |
91: | Module/service boundaries, scaling, system design | [architecture](references/architecture.md) |
92: | Screens, user flow, responsive behavior, keyboard/screen-reader | [ui-ux-accessibility](references/ui-ux-accessibility.md) |
93: | Crash, regression, wrong output (default); non-deterministic, concurrent, or toolchain-level root cause | [debugging](references/debugging.md); add [advanced debugging](references/debugging-advanced.md) only for the second case |
94: | Test plan, coverage, acceptance criteria (default); property/fuzz/contract harness implementation | [testing-qa](references/testing-qa.md); add [test engineering](references/test-engineering.md) only for the second case |
95: | Latency, throughput, memory, CPU, startup, frame time | [performance](references/performance.md) |
96: | Build, package, workflow, deployment, CI/CD (default); compiler/linker/toolchain internals | [devops-ci-cd](references/devops-ci-cd.md); add [build/toolchain](references/build-toolchain-engineering.md) only for the second case |
97: | Persistence/serialization contract (default); schema/query behaviour; wire-format/endpoint contract | [data-api](references/data-api.md); [database engineering](references/database-engineering.md) for schema/query; [API/protocol engineering](references/api-protocol-engineering.md) for wire format |
98: | Review, cleanup, behavior-preserving refactor | [review-refactor](references/review-refactor.md) |
99: | README, API docs, ADR, runbook, changelog | [documentation](references/documentation.md) |
100: | SSR/hydration, service workers, browser storage, edge or browser-runtime boundaries | [web platform engineering](references/web-platform-engineering.md) |
101: | Version uncertainty, external claims, unsupported tools | [verification](references/verification.md) |

104: 
105: Start with [programming language routing](references/programming-languages.md), then load only what matches the repository. 107: - [C/C++/Rust and systems programming](references/systems-programming.md)
108: - [Python](references/python-engineering.md)
109: - [JavaScript/TypeScript/Node.js](references/javascript-typescript.md)
110: - [.NET/C#/Java/JVM](references/dotnet-java-engineering.md)
111: - [Go](references/go-engineering.md)
112: - [Frontend and browser engineering](references/frontend-engineering.md)
113: - [Backend and service engineering](references/backend-api-engineering.md)
114: - [Mobile engineering](references/mobile-engineering.md)
115: - [Game, emulator, and real-time engines](references/game-engineering.md)
116: - [Embedded and firmware](references/embedded-engineering.md)
117: - [Machine learning and AI systems](references/ml-ai-engineering.md)
118: - [Functional and reactive programming](references/functional-programming.md)
119: - [Distributed systems](references/distributed-systems-engineering.md)
120: 
121: ### Cybersecurity and defensive operations
122: 
123: Start with [security](references/security.md) as the framing owner and keep it loaded alongside the narrowest technical specialist below (do not substitute the narrow specialist for the base):
124: 
125: - [Threat modeling](references/threat-modeling.md) and [secure code review](references/secure-code-review.md)
126: - [Application security](references/application-security.md) and [authorized penetration testing](references/penetration-testing.md)
127: - [Cloud, container, and infrastructure security](references/cloud-container-security.md)
128: - [Network and protocol security](references/network-security.md)
129: - [Identity, cryptography, and secrets](references/identity-crypto-secrets.md) plus [applied cryptography](references/cryptography-engineering.md)
130: - [Software supply-chain security](references/supply-chain-security.md)
131: - [Vulnerability research and responsible disclosure](references/vulnerability-research.md)
132: - [Incident response and digital forensics](references/incident-response-forensics.md)
133: - [Malware triage and analysis](references/malware-analysis.md), strictly for defensive understanding and containment
134: - [Binary exploitation mitigation and hardening](references/binary-exploitation-defense.md)
135: - [Smart contract security](references/smart-contract-security.md)
136: 
137: ### Reverse engineering and interoperability
138: 
139: Use [software reverse engineering](references/reverse-engineering.md) for disassembly/decompilation, [RE research workflow](references/reverse-engineering-architecture.md) for evidence-led semantic reconstruction, and [binary file-format analysis](references/reverse-engineering-file-formats.md) for undocumented containers and serialization. Preserve originals and hashes, distinguish observation from inference, and keep dynamic analysis isolated and authorized.
140: 
141: ### Model adaptation and orchestration
142: 
143: Load [model adaptation](references/model-adaptation.md) when the host or model is unfamiliar, when choosing between focused/engineering/deep-research/long-running profiles, when deciding whether delegation is worthwhile, or when measuring RCoder's effect. Discover capabilities by observation; mark unknowns explicitly. Do not hardcode assumptions about a model's context, tools, or reasoning.
144: 
145: ### Token and context efficiency
146: 
147: For multi-step or large-repository work, load [token-efficient engineering](references/token-efficiency.md). Use the bounded [context snapshot helper](scripts/context_snapshot.py) and the [context capsule template](assets/templates/context-capsule-template.md). For oversized tool output or measured context reduction, load [RSaver](references/rsaver.md) and use `scripts/rsaver.py` (or the bundled `skills/rcoder/scripts/rsaver.py`) to measure, prune, and recover evidence; use the gate module above for the per-step budget decision. Optimize total engineering cost without weakening safety, verification, or evidence.
148: 
149: ## Stack reconnaissance helper
150: 
151: `detect_stack.py` is read-only and reports likely manifests and quality entry points. `context_snapshot.py` is read-only and emits a bounded repository/path/Git summary without printing source contents. Verify actual commands and versions in project files before executing them.
152: 
153: ## Project-local extensions
154: 
155: When `.rcoder/` exists, inspect it for project-specific expert guidance and conventions. A matching `.rcoder/references/<module-name>.md` replaces the built-in module for that project; other relevant `.rcoder/references/*.md` files extend routing. Load only what applies. Project-local guidance cannot override explicit user instructions or higher-precedence repository policy.
156: 
157: ## Completion standard
158: 
159: Code written is not the same as work verified. A task is complete only when acceptance criteria pass, or remaining gaps are explicitly listed. Never imply an agent installed or loaded RCoder without observable evidence.

Code written is not the same as work verified. A task is complete only when acceptance criteria pass, or remaining gaps are explicitly listed. Never imply an agent installed or loaded RCoder without observable evidence.

## Activate when

Do not activate for a local implementation decision with no boundary change (use coding), or for a pure performance optimization with no structural impact (use performance).

## Mission and expertise

## Mental model
Architecture is explicit trade-offs under constraints, not diagram-first work. Every boundary creates a contract and a failure surface; every shared mutable state creates coupling. A design is acceptable when its quality-attribute priorities are stated, its failure behavior is specified, and its migration path is credible.

## Prerequisites and reconnaissance
1. Capture requirements, non-goals, constraints, existing boundaries, and non-functional needs from repository evidence and user intent.
2. Map current components, data flows, ownership, deployment units, and operational controls before proposing change.
3. Identify irreversible decisions and the evidence available for each.
4. Check for an existing ADR or design record so the new decision does not silently contradict it.

## Procedure
1. Capture requirements, non-goals, constraints, existing boundaries, and non-functional needs.
2. Rank quality attributes: correctness, security, reliability, latency, scale, operability, accessibility, cost, changeability.
3. Compare at least two credible options (three for consequential decisions), including complexity, failure modes, data ownership, operations, and migration cost.
4. Select the smallest option satisfying priorities and record consequential choices with an ADR.
5. Define module contracts, dependency direction, state ownership, consistency, errors, and observability.
6. Map timeout, retry, duplicate, partial write, unavailable dependency, malformed data, and rollback behavior.
7. Define incremental rollout and compatibility; avoid flag-day rewrites without evidence.

## Decision tree
- Single process, bounded data, one team → prefer modular monolith boundaries over service split.
- Independent scaling/deployment or distinct trust boundary is required → justify a service boundary and define its contract and failure mode first.
- Strong consistency is required across a boundary → keep ownership co-located or use a transaction strategy with explicit failure semantics.
- Eventual consistency is acceptable → define idempotency, ordering, deduplication, and reconciliation rules.
- Existing system is poorly understood → characterize behavior first; do not design a replacement from assumptions.
- Decision is hard to reverse or crosses a security boundary → write an ADR and require explicit review.
- Options are indistinguishable on evidence → choose the simplest reversible option and state what would change the decision.

## Tool strategy
Use dependency graphs, import/link analysis, and architecture tests to make boundaries visible and enforceable. Use ADRs (template available under `assets/templates/`) for consequential decisions. Use prototypes or spikes only when they answer a specific risk question. Verify operational claims against the actual deployment configuration rather than documentation.

## Advanced techniques
- **Quality-attribute scenarios:** express each priority as "under stimulus X, the system responds within Y" so trade-offs become testable.
- **Failure-mode enumeration:** for each boundary, list timeouts, duplicates, partial failures, stale state, and recovery, then design for them.
- **Ownership maps:** assign each piece of state a single writer and define how readers handle stale or missing data.
- **Strangler-style migration:** route a bounded slice at a time behind a stable interface; keep rollback possible at each step.
- **Architecture fitness functions:** encode forbidden dependencies or layer violations as automated checks.
- **Cost of change analysis:** prefer the option that keeps the most likely future change local.

## Failure modes
- **Premature distribution** → network failure and operational cost without need → consolidate behind module boundaries first.
- **Diagram-as-proof** → attractive design with unspecified failure semantics → write contracts and failure tables.
- **Speculative abstraction** → layers no caller needs → add abstraction only with two real use cases.
- **Hidden shared mutable state** → coupling and races → make ownership explicit and single-writer.
- **Flag-day rewrite** → high-risk cutover with no rollback → migrate incrementally with compatibility shims.

## Quality checklist
Boundaries and data ownership are explicit; failure behavior and recovery are specified; security/trust boundaries and operations are visible; evolution and migration path are credible; quality priorities are ranked and traceable to the decision.

## Anti-patterns
Designing for hypothetical scale; copying another organization's topology; distributed transactions without a failure analysis; storing the same authoritative state in multiple services; hiding operational complexity in an ADR footnote.

## Verification
Review dependency graphs and architecture fitness checks, validate contract/migration tests with fixtures, and exercise one end-to-end path plus one failure path. Confirm the design satisfies the ranked quality attributes with evidence; mark unmeasured attributes NOT VERIFIED.

## Output format
Requirements · quality priorities · options/trade-offs · ADR · contracts/failure modes · evolution plan · residual risks.

# ADR-001: Real-time delivery architecture for client push updates

- Status: Proposed
- Date: 2026-11-19
- Owners: Platform / Real-time service team
- Decision scope: Pre-implementation architecture choice; no code exists yet.

## Assumptions (reversible, stated because the request is underspecified)

The request names "two real-time service architectures" without a domain, scale, or
quality targets, and the fixture contains no source, manifests, or deployment config.
To make the comparison concrete and checkable, this ADR assumes:

- A1: The dominant traffic pattern is server-to-client push of time-ordered events
  (notifications, activity feeds, presence/status, live metric updates) to browser
  and mobile clients.
- A2: Client-to-server messages are low-frequency and tolerate ordinary HTTP latency
  (acks, subscriptions, commands). True low-latency bidirectional interaction
  (multiplayer gaming, collaborative text editing) is NOT a driver.
- A3: Clients run behind corporate proxies, NAT, and CDNs; traffic must traverse
  standard HTTPS (443) without special firewall rules.
- A4: Peak concurrency is moderate (order of 10^4–10^5 simultaneous clients), with
  bursty fanout to subsets of clients.
- A5: The team optimizes for operability and cost over absolute minimum latency;
  end-to-end push latency of roughly a few hundred milliseconds is acceptable.
- A6: An existing managed message broker (Kafka or Redis Pub/Sub class) is available
  as the authoritative event backbone.

Evidence status: these are **INFERRED** working assumptions, not repository facts.
If any is false, re-open this ADR before implementation; see "What would change this
decision."

## Context and constraints

We must deliver live updates to many concurrent clients. The service boundary is the
connection/edge layer between an internal event backbone and external clients. Every
choice here creates a long-lived operational contract: connection lifecycle,
backpressure, reconnection, and a trust boundary at the public edge. There is no
existing real-time implementation or prior ADR to preserve, so this is a greenfield,
hard-to-reverse decision and is documented before implementation.

Non-goals: choosing the internal event producer design; defining business-event
schemas; building git-based CI/CD (covered elsewhere).

## Decision drivers (ranked quality attributes)

1. Operability and failure recovery — reconnect, backpressure, observability, rolling
   deploys without dropping clients.
2. Reliability under fanout — no lost/duplicated events, bounded ordering guarantees.
3. Network compatibility — works through proxies, CDNs, HTTP/2, standard TLS.
4. Cost and scaling efficiency — edge should be stateless/horizontally scalable where
   possible.
5. Security — authenticated edge, input validation, no exposed internal topology.
6. Latency — important but secondary under A5 (target: hundreds of ms, not sub-50 ms).
7. Changeability — client contract stable, migration possible without flag day.

Quality-attribute scenarios (testable):
- QAS-1 (reliability): "When a client disconnects mid-stream and reconnects within 60 s,
  it resumes without missing or duplicating events beyond the documented at-least-once
  contract."
- QAS-2 (operability): "During a rolling deploy of the edge tier, no established client
  session is forcibly terminated."
- QAS-3 (compatibility): "A client behind a standard HTTPS-only corporate proxy can
  establish and maintain a push channel over port 443 with no extra firewall rule."

## Options and trade-offs

**Option A — Stateful WebSocket gateway with in-process fanout.**
A dedicated gateway tier holds persistent, full-duplex WebSocket connections. Each
gateway subscribes to the event backbone, keeps a local registry of connection ->
subscription interests, and fans events out over open sockets. Routing may require a
connection-ownership map or sticky routing so a client's events reach the gateway that
holds its socket.

**Option B — SSE edge over HTTP with a managed pub/sub backbone.**
Clients open a unidirectional `text/event-stream` HTTP connection (SSE) to a stateless
edge tier; the edge bridges broker subscriptions to the response stream. Browser
clients reconnect and resume automatically via the native EventSource API with
`Last-Event-ID`. Client-to-server traffic uses ordinary authenticated HTTP POST. HTTP/2
multiplexes many streams per connection.

| Option | Benefits | Costs and risks |
|---|---|---|
| A — WebSocket gateway | True full-duplex, lowest per-message latency; efficient for high-frequency bidirectional traffic; single connection for both directions | Stateful edge => hard horizontal scaling and sticky routing; connection-ownership map is a new failure surface; proxy/upgrade handling and heartbeat/timeout tuning; manual reconnect/resume logic; rolling deploys can drop sockets; more operational surface |
| B — SSE + managed pub/sub | Stateless, horizontally scalable edge; native browser auto-reconnect and `Last-Event-ID` resume; HTTP/2 multiplexing; traverses proxies/CDNs and standard 443; simpler security model (plain HTTP auth); reuses the existing broker | Unidirectional server->client (client messages via HTTP POST); text-only payloads (binary needs encoding); browser per-origin connection-limit concerns on HTTP/1.1; slightly higher per-message overhead; historical HTTP/1.1 connection caps mitigated by HTTP/2 |

## Failure-mode comparison

| Failure mode | Option A (WebSocket) | Option B (SSE + broker) |
|---|---|---|
| Client drop / reconnect | App-level heartbeat + custom resume; easy to lose events | Native EventSource reconnect + `Last-Event-ID` resume |
| Backpressure | Must buffer per-socket; slow clients can exhaust gateway memory | Backpressure at edge/stream; broker lag is observable and shared |
| Rolling deploy | Open sockets can be severed; needs drain/connection migration | Stateless edge; clients reconnect transparently |
| Duplicate/lost events | Custom sequencing required | Broker offset + `Last-Event-ID` give explicit at-least-once semantics |
| Proxy/firewall | Upgrade handshake can be blocked | Plain HTTPS long-lived response; broadly compatible |
| Partial broker outage | Gateway-local registry may diverge | Edge is disposable; state stays in broker |

## Decision

We select **Option B — SSE over HTTP with the managed pub/sub backbone**, as the
smallest option that satisfies the ranked drivers under assumptions A1–A6. It keeps the
edge stateless (drivers 1, 4), leverages native reconnect/resume and broker offsets for
reliable delivery (driver 2), and traverses the deployment network without special
rules (drivers 3, 5). It is the more reversible choice: the client contract is plain
HTTP and can later be supplemented with a WebSocket path for a specific bidirectional
feature without replacing the backbone.

This decision is INFERRED from the stated assumptions, not VERIFIED against a running
system (none exists in the fixture).

## Consequences and verification

### Positive
- Horizontally scalable, disposable edge; simpler deploy and incident recovery.
- Built-in browser reconnect and resume reduce custom client code and event loss.
- Reuses the existing broker as the single authoritative event source; no duplicate
  authoritative state at the edge.

### Negative / accepted costs
- No low-latency client->server channel; client input goes over HTTP POST (acceptable
  under A2, unacceptable if A2 is false).
- Text-only streams; binary payloads require base64 or a separate mechanism.
- Must manage HTTP/1.1 per-origin connection limits; rely on HTTP/2 where available.
- `Last-Event-ID` resume requires broker retention long enough to cover expected
  disconnect windows.

### Contract and observability to implement
- Single writer for event state: the broker. Edge holds no authoritative state.
- At-least-once delivery; clients must deduplicate by event ID. Define ordering scope
  (per subscription key) explicitly.
- Headers/fields: `event:`, `id:`, `data:`, `retry:`; `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect.
- Auth at edge before subscribing; validate subscription scope server-side.
- Metrics: active streams, broker consumer lag, reconnect rate, resume success rate,
  event age at delivery. Alerts on lag and reconnect spikes.

### Verification plan (required before go-live; all currently NOT VERIFIED)
- V1: Integration test for QAS-1 — kill a stream, reconnect with `Last-Event-ID`, assert
  no missed/duplicated events beyond the documented contract.
- V2: Deploy test for QAS-2 — rolling-restart the edge tier and assert no forced client
  session termination and clean reconnects.
- V3: Network test for QAS-3 — connect from behind an HTTPS-only proxy and confirm the
  stream establishes over 443.
- V4: Load/fanout test at A4 scale — measure lag, edge CPU/memory, and p95 event age.
- V5: Failure test — simulate broker partition and slow clients; confirm bounded
  backpressure and no state divergence.
- V6: Security review of edge auth and subscription authorization.

## Evolution / rollout plan

1. Ship the SSE edge behind a flag for a single non-critical event type; keep the old
   notification path (if any) as the fallback.
2. Validate V1–V6; ramp traffic by cohort with rollback via flag to the prior path.
3. Standardize the client SDK on EventSource semantics and event-ID deduplication.
4. Revisit only if a driver changes (see below); introduce a WebSocket path as a
   complementary, bounded feature rather than a wholesale replacement.

## Residual risks

- A2/A4/A5 are assumptions; if bidirectional low-latency or far higher scale is real,
  the decision may be wrong — re-open before implementation.
- Broker retention must be provisioned to satisfy QAS-1; undersizing causes resume gaps.
- HTTP/1.1 client connection limits in older mobile clients may require HTTP/2 or
  domain sharding.
- No measured latency/scale data exists yet; all quality attributes remain NOT VERIFIED
  until V1–V6 run.

## What would change this decision

Switch to **Option A (WebSocket)** if any of the following becomes a confirmed driver:
- high-frequency, low-latency client->server messaging (collaborative editing, gaming);
- hard sub-50 ms end-to-end latency requirement;
- binary streaming as a first-class payload;
- a proven proxy environment that blocks long-lived SSE but permits WebSocket upgrade.

Record such a change as a new ADR that supersedes this one; do not silently overwrite
this record.
